sources.entry: Hardware Store Elimination - Finds an undocumented optimisation by its counter signature and bandwidth, and sets the method for what manuals omit.

summary.title: Hardware Store Elimination
summary.one_liner: Writing zeros over zero-filled cache lines on Skylake client Intel CPUs can be partly eliminated in hardware, cutting L3 and memory writes and speeding up large fills compared with writing ones.
takeaways: On an Intel Skylake client chip, storing zeros over lines that are already zero was about 17-18% faster than storing ones in the L3 and RAM regions, with identical machine code.
Performance counters show that many zero-over-zero writes are evicted silently from L2 and never written back, roughly halving writes to L3 and memory.
The elimination only applied to about 40-60% of redundant lines and did not apply to alternating zero/one lines, so the exact mechanism remains unknown.
The effect was not observed on other Intel (Haswell, Skylake-X), AMD Zen2, POWER9 or Graviton 2 hardware tested, so it may be Skylake client specific.
summary.summary: The author benchmarks a simple AVX2 fill function on gcc 9.2.1 and finds that filling buffers with zero is consistently about 17-18% faster than filling with one once the data exceeds L2, even though the machine code is identical. Using Intel L2 eviction events (l2_lines_out.silent and non_silent) and uncore write counters, they show that zero-over-zero lines are often dropped silently, so about half as many writes reach L3 and memory. The post then tests predictor-based theories with an alternating zero/one variant and surveys other Intel, AMD, POWER9 and ARM chips, where the effect was not seen. The author labels the mechanism speculative and leaves its exact trigger unresolved.
